title: Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)
hook: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and how to play it well

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night before Holi: the bonfire, and Prahlada walking out of the flames. Your line was still saying the name.

The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. The next morning, the street belongs to color. Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink. For the colors, people tell a different, smaller story, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.
screen: `THE ASH, CARRIED HOME.` → `WHY COLOR?` → `A SECOND, SMALLER STORY.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark; the old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud. The story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark? Yashoda laughs: go and put some color on her face, then. So he does, and Radha and her friends put color right back on him. That's the game. It's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture. But in Braj it's everything. The towns tied to Krishna and Radha keep Holi for days. In Barsana, Radha's village in the stories, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh. In Vrindavan, some temples throw flower petals instead of powder. How do people play? The color is gulal, a soft powder. The old colors came from flowers, like the orange of the palash tree, soaked overnight; some families have gone back to gentle, natural colors. You start with elders: a pinch of color on their feet or cheeks, and a bow. You say happy Holi before you throw. You don't color someone who's said no, or a stranger who's clearly just trying to get to work. Then there's food: gujiya, little fried pastries full of sweet milk and nuts, and cool thandai to drink. The color is a greeting. Krishna didn't throw it to win. He threw it to close a distance, and he laughed when it came back.
screen: `A DARK BOY WORRIED ABOUT HIS SKIN.` · `GO AND COLOR HER FACE, THEN.` · `BRAJ KEEPS HOLI FOR DAYS.` · `ELDERS FIRST. ASK. THEN THROW.` · then, large: `COLOR CLOSES A DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you feel a little distance from: not an enemy, just someone you drifted from, or have been a bit cold with. Picture walking up to them on Holi morning; you say happy Holi first, wait for them to smile, then a small pinch of pink on their cheek. Then picture them putting color right back on you, both of you laughing, the same messy color.
Holi. The spring festival: the fire the night before, for Prahlada, and the colors in the morning, for Krishna and Radha.
Your line: color closes a distance. Tomorrow, nine nights begin. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

howItsDone: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj the celebrations run for days.

notes: The Yashoda/Radha 'why is Radha fair and I'm dark' story is presented as a story families and songs tell, not scripture. Confirm framing.
'The old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud' (megha-shyama); a common epithet. Confirm.
Lathmar Holi: women of Barsana and men of Nandgaon (Krishna's village). Described without naming Nandgaon. Confirm.
Ash carried home from Holika Dahan and touched to the forehead: a regional custom, not universal. Confirm wording.
Palash (tesu) flowers as a traditional color source. Confirm.

The index carry for this camp-3 festival run repeats the title ('Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)'), which reads awkwardly as 'your line'. Kept exactly; the owner may want a shorter carry in the outline.

Etymology of 'Holi': the link to Holika is popular but debated (other derivations, e.g. from 'hola', roasted grain, are proposed). The original note was softened from 'from the name of Holika' to 'often linked to Holika'. Confirm.
